136.title: Governance
136.description: Igris's governance model gives you verifiable, auditable records of every AI decision. Governance applies to every execution, whether running on cloud or local hardware.
136.content: Governance What Governance Covers Execution Receipts Capability Model Agent Lifecycle Transaction Boundary Routing Policy Trust Chain Compliance Use Cases Setting Up Governance for Your Fleet Step 1 — Define your capability policy Step 2 — Assign policies to agents Step 3 — Monitor violations Step 4 — Review receipts for compliance Step 5 — Adjust and iterate # Governance Igris's governance model gives you verifiable, auditable records of every AI decision. Governance applies to every execution, whether running on cloud or local hardware. --- ## What Governance Covers Governance answers three questions: 1. **What happened?** Every execution produces a signed receipt with inputs, outputs, timing, and resource use. 2. **Was it within bounds?** Capability gates enforce declared limits before and during execution. 3. **Can it be verified?** Receipts are cryptographically signed and tamper-evident. --- ## Execution Receipts Every execution produces a receipt: a structured, signed record of the full execution. Receipts contain: - The original request (inputs) - The response (outputs) - Resource usage: tokens consumed, time elapsed, tool calls made - Which capability gates were active - A cryptographic signature over the canonical envelope Receipts are stored locally on the execution engine. They can be queried via API and exported for audit workflows. [Execution Receipts →](/docs/execution-receipts) --- ## Capability Model Igris enforces a capability model: every execution declares what it is permitted to do, and the engine rejects operations outside that scope before they complete. Capability grants control what an execution is permitted to do: | Capability | What it controls | |---|---| | `allow_http` | Whether the agent can make outbound HTTP calls | | `allowed_http_domains` | Allowlist of domains for HTTP calls | | `allow_shell` | Whether the agent can execute shell commands | | `allow_filesystem` | Whether the agent can read or write files | | `max_file_write_bytes` | Maximum bytes the execution may write | Execution resource limits (max tokens, max steps, max wall time) are set separately in your containment policy and apply regardless of capability grants. A request that exceeds its capability grant is rejected before the operation executes. The rejection is recorded in the execution receipt. [Capability Model →](/docs/capability-model) --- ## Agent Lifecycle Igris tracks the lifecycle of agent executions: creation, active execution, completion, and termination. Lifecycle events are recorded in the execution envelope and available via the observability API. For long-running agents, Igris enforces: - Heartbeat requirements - Maximum active duration - Graceful shutdown on deadline [Agent Lifecycle →](/docs/agent-l

138.title: Hybrid Deployment Workflow
138.description: Use this workflow when you want one product experience for the customer while combining the hosted API with one or more local runtimes.
138.content: Hybrid Deployment Workflow 1. Keep the application pointed at the hosted API 2. Start runtimes with registration credentials 3. Verify cloud and runtime access separately 4. Use fleet APIs for coordination 5. Separate hot-path traffic from provisioning traffic Common Mistakes Related Guides # Hybrid Deployment Workflow Use this workflow when you want one product experience for the customer while combining the hosted API with one or more local runtimes. This is the right model when you want: - hosted API access for the application layer - local runtime execution close to the device or workload - fleet visibility and rollout control - a fallback path between hosted and local execution --- ## 1. Keep the application pointed at the hosted API The application-facing base URL stays the same: text https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1 That keeps the customer contract unified even when runtimes are participating underneath. The application continues to see one product API, while Igris decides where execution and coordination should happen. ## 2. Start runtimes with registration credentials Hybrid deployment only works when the runtime can register successfully. bash export IGRIS_LICENSE_KEY="YOUR_LICENSE_KEY" export IGRIS_API_KEY="YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY" igris-runtime serve ## 3. Verify cloud and runtime access separately Confirm both sides independently: - hosted API calls succeed with your tenant API key - the runtime answers `http://localhost:8080/v1/health` - fleet visibility appears in the console when registration succeeds ## 4. Use fleet APIs for coordination Once runtimes are participating, use the documented fleet-management routes and workflows for: - runtime inventory - config push - OTA updates Do not rebuild a parallel coordination system when the product surface already supports it. Hybrid works best when the application path stays simple and device operations stay explicit. ## 5. Separate hot-path traffic from provisioning traffic Keep the hosted inference path and runtime management path conceptually separate: - application traffic calls the hosted API - operators and rollout systems manage runtimes and fleet operations That keeps the architecture readable, makes failure handling clearer, and avoids treating device management like ordinary inference traffic. ## Common Mistakes - Pointing application clients directly at runtime coordination routes - Expecting fleet visibility without valid `IGRIS_LICENSE_KEY` and `IGRIS_API_KEY` - Mixing rollout traffic and customer inference traffic into the same operational path ## Related Guides - [Quick Start →](/docs/quickstart) - [Fleet Management →](/docs/fleet-management) - [Cloud Coordination →](/do

139.title: Identity & Access
139.description: How Igris handles console identity, tenant API keys, tenant roles, and higher-assurance access controls.
139.content: Identity & Access Two Access Planes Console Identity Tenant API Keys Tenant Roles Higher-Assurance Access Controls 2FA SSO Recommended Operating Model Related Pages # Identity & Access Igris separates **human access** from **programmatic access**. - **Console identity** is for people using the web app - **Tenant API keys** are for applications, automation, and deployed runtimes Treat those as different contracts. --- ## Two Access Planes | Plane | Used by | Primary credential | Scope | |---|---|---|---| | **Console** | Human operators | Session cookie | Browser session tied to a tenant user | | **API** | Apps, agents, runtimes | `igris_` API key | Tenant-scoped machine access | Console cookies are not a published bearer-token contract. For scripts and integrations, use tenant API keys. --- ## Console Identity The console uses a session-based sign-in model. A user signs in once, receives a session cookie, and then operates inside one tenant context at a time. Current product behavior: - Console access is designed for interactive human use - Session state is separate from tenant API-key auth - Tenant context is applied before policy, billing, and audit logic This keeps browser access and machine access cleanly separated. --- ## Tenant API Keys Tenant API keys are the automation contract for the coordination layer. Accepted forms: - `Authorization: Bearer YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY` - `X-API-Key: YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY` Use tenant API keys for: - server-side application calls - CI/CD or operational automation - provisioning and runtime registration flows - customer-visible integrations that should not depend on browser cookies Do not reuse one tenant's API key across other tenants. Keys are tenant-scoped by design. --- ## Tenant Roles Igris distinguishes between ordinary tenant access and elevated administrative access. In practical terms, roles matter for: - tenant administration - sensitive configuration changes - identity and security operations - management actions that should not be available to every authenticated caller When you design operational workflows, treat roles as part of the product boundary that customers and operators can reason about directly. --- ## Higher-Assurance Access Controls Igris includes stronger access controls for deployments that need more than basic session auth plus API keys. ### 2FA Two-factor authentication is available for tenant-level console access hardening. Use it when console operators can perform security-sensitive actions such as reviewing paused executions, rotating provider keys, or chang

140.title: Key Management
140.description: Igris stores provider keys in the vault used by the cloud coordination layer.
140.content: Key Management What The Current Public API Supports Add A Provider Key Rotate, Validate, Remove Security Properties # Key Management Igris stores provider keys in the vault used by the cloud coordination layer. --- ## What The Current Public API Supports The current public vault API accepts these provider identifiers: | Provider | Intended use | |---|---| | `openai` | Customer cloud traffic | | `anthropic` | Customer cloud traffic | | `benchmark` | Synthetic or test traffic | Do not assume broader provider coverage on the public vault API unless it is explicitly documented in the current contract. --- ## Add A Provider Key bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/vault/keys \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "provider": "openai", "key_name": "production", "api_key": "YOUR_OPENAI_KEY" }' Current request fields: | Field | Description | |---|---| | `provider` | Provider identifier such as `openai` | | `key_name` | Human-readable name for the key | | `api_key` | Provider secret to encrypt and store | --- ## Rotate, Validate, Remove Current routes: - `GET /v1/vault/keys` - `GET /v1/vault/keys/:provider` - `POST /v1/vault/keys/:provider/rotate` - `POST /v1/vault/keys/:provider/validate` - `DELETE /v1/vault/keys/:provider` The current response contract returns masked values only. Raw provider secrets are never returned after creation. --- ## Security Properties - Provider keys are encrypted before storage - Key operations are tenant-scoped - API responses expose masked key material only - Vault operations are available through authenticated control-plane APIs --- [Cloud Coordination →](/docs/cloud-coordination) · [Security →](/docs/security) · [API Reference →](/docs/api-reference)

141.title: Licensing & Activation
141.description: How Igris licenses are activated, validated, and kept alive across the console, coordination layer, and deployed runtimes.
141.content: Licensing & Activation Product Model Tenant Activation Runtime Admission Device Identity And Heartbeats What The License Controls Recommended Operating Model Related Pages # Licensing & Activation Igris licensing is not just a billing flag. It is part of the runtime bootstrap path. There are two distinct surfaces: - **Tenant activation in the console** associates a purchased license with a tenant - **Runtime validation and heartbeat** determine whether a deployed runtime is allowed to stay active Treat those as one lifecycle. --- ## Product Model At a high level, the licensing flow works like this: 1. A tenant activates a license key from the console. 2. The runtime validates that license during startup. 3. The runtime registers a device identity under that license. 4. The runtime sends periodic heartbeats to remain counted as active. If validation fails, the runtime should not be treated as fully admitted into the platform. --- ## Tenant Activation The console exposes a tenant-facing activation flow so an operator can bind a license to the current tenant account. From a product perspective, that does three things: - sets the active plan for the tenant - determines the feature set and quota envelope - establishes the license record that runtimes will validate against The console also exposes plan and quota state, including: - current plan - license status - request quota - device quota - active device count That means licensing is visible to both finance and operations, not just procurement. --- ## Runtime Admission The runtime performs license validation during startup before it proceeds with its normal cloud-registration path. In practical terms, runtime admission depends on: - a valid license key - a generated device identity - the runtime version reported during validation The runtime then attempts device registration under that license. This is important operationally because a license is not only "valid" or "invalid"; it also tracks how many active devices are attached to it. --- ## Device Identity And Heartbeats Each runtime derives a device ID from local machine characteristics and registers that device against the license. Once registered, the runtime sends periodic heartbeats. This gives Igris an operational answer to questions like: - which runtimes are still alive - how many devices are currently consuming the license - whether a device should be treated as stale or deregistered If you are operating a fleet, heartbeats are part of capacity accounting, not just health reporting. --- ## What The License Controls Lice

142.title: Local LLM Fallback
142.description: igris-runtime can serve GGUF models locally and participate in hybrid deployments where cloud routing falls back to on-device inference.
142.content: Local LLM Fallback What Exists Today Configuration Fields Hybrid Behavior Supported Model Format Operational Notes # Local LLM Fallback `igris-runtime` can serve GGUF models locally and participate in hybrid deployments where cloud routing falls back to on-device inference. --- ## What Exists Today The current runtime config surface is `local_fallback`. The shipped config supports local model loading and tuning knobs such as context size, threading, GPU layer offload, and prompt caching. json5 { local_fallback: { enabled: true, model_path: "/models/mistral-7b.Q4_K_M.gguf", context_size: 4096, threads: 4, n_gpu_layers: 0, max_tokens: 512, temperature: 0.7 } } Optional fields also available in the current runtime: - `main_gpu` - `prompt_cache_dir` - `batch_size` - `lora_adapter_path` --- ## Configuration Fields | Field | Description | |---|---| | `enabled` | Enables the local fallback subsystem | | `model_path` | Path to the GGUF model on disk | | `context_size` | Runtime context window size | | `threads` | CPU threads for local inference | | `n_gpu_layers` | Number of model layers offloaded to GPU | | `max_tokens` | Default local generation cap | | `temperature` | Default local sampling temperature | There is no dedicated pure-local fallback toggle in the current runtime config. For pure local deployments, point clients directly at `http://localhost:8080/v1` and do not rely on cloud routing. --- ## Hybrid Behavior In a hybrid deployment: 1. Your application calls Overture 2. Overture routes normally across cloud providers 3. If the runtime is registered and selected by your routing configuration, local execution can participate in the request path In a fully local deployment: 1. Your application calls the runtime directly 2. The runtime answers from the local model 3. Signed execution receipts are returned with the response payload when enabled by the runtime path --- ## Supported Model Format The current runtime expects GGUF model files on disk. Choose a model size that matches your hardware budget. | Hardware | Suggested starting point | |---|---| | CPU-only edge box | Phi-3 Mini or other compact GGUF | | Apple Silicon laptop | 7B to 8B GGUF models | | Dedicated GPU host | Larger GGUF models with `n_gpu_layers` tuned upward | --- ## Operational Notes - Local inference availability is controlled by the runtime process, not by a separate cloud toggle - Console-side fleet visibility requires successful runtime registration; local inference itself does not - When you call t

143.title: MCP
143.description: Context Engineering → · MCP Server → · API Reference →
143.content: MCP Guide Pages Transport Surfaces Method Families Session and Transport Context and Resource Operations Tooling and Agent Workflows How MCP Fits In # MCP MCP is the structured context layer in Igris. Use it when context belongs to the operating environment and must move between tools, agents, sessions, or runtimes without becoming accidental prompt state. This section documents MCP as part of the product contract. Start with the overview pages below if you are orienting yourself, then move to the transport and integration guides when you are shaping production workflows. ## Guide Pages - [MCP Server](/docs/mcp-server): customer-facing transport and method model - [MCP Swarm Mode](/docs/mcp-swarm): how shared context behaves in multi-agent execution - [MCP Integration Patterns](/docs/mcp-integration-patterns): practical patterns for durable, auditable context usage ## Transport Surfaces - [`POST /v1/mcp`](/docs/mcp-server): hosted transport for customer-facing MCP requests - [`POST /v1/mcp/stream`](/docs/mcp-server): streaming transport when MCP exchange needs incremental output ## Method Families ### Session and Transport - initialize session state - advertise capabilities - establish request and response shape ### Context and Resource Operations - list available context resources - read resource content - push or refresh context into the shared working surface ### Tooling and Agent Workflows - expose tools to participating agents - share execution context across swarm members - coordinate working context without confusing it with receipts or durable checkpoints ## How MCP Fits In Use MCP for shared working context. Use durable tasks for long-running progress. Use receipts for audit evidence. Keeping those three concerns separate is what makes the system understandable and operable at scale. --- [Context Engineering →](/docs/context-engineering) · [MCP Server →](/docs/mcp-server) · [API Reference →](/docs/api-reference)

144.title: MCP Integration Patterns
144.description: This guide shows how to use MCP as part of a production integration rather than as an isolated protocol feature.
144.content: MCP Integration Patterns Pattern: Separate Working Context From Audit Data Pattern: Give Shared Context A Schema Pattern: Pair MCP With Durable Tasks Deliberately Pattern: Keep The Product Boundary Clean Related Guides # MCP Integration Patterns This guide shows how to use MCP as part of a production integration rather than as an isolated protocol feature. --- ## Pattern: Separate Working Context From Audit Data Use MCP for working state that tools, agents, or runtimes need to share. Do not use MCP as the place where audit evidence lives. Keep audit and receipt workflows separate so the system remains understandable. ## Pattern: Give Shared Context A Schema Avoid dumping arbitrary JSON into a few generic keys. Define stable keys and value shapes for shared context that your application team can reason about. Good: - `mission_state` - `dispatch_plan` - `device_role` Weak: - `state` - `payload` - `latest_data` ## Pattern: Pair MCP With Durable Tasks Deliberately MCP and durable tasks solve different problems: - MCP shares structured state - durable tasks preserve progress and resume semantics Use both when a long-running workflow needs shared context and safe recovery. Do not force one to replace the other. ## Pattern: Keep The Product Boundary Clean Your application should still think in terms of one product: - hosted coordination when the application contract belongs in the cloud - runtime-local execution when work belongs on-device - MCP for shared operational state across those boundaries ## Related Guides - [MCP →](/docs/mcp) - [MCP Server →](/docs/mcp-server) - [Durable Tasks →](/docs/durable-tasks) - [Context Engineering →](/docs/context-engineering)

145.title: MCP Server
145.description: This page documents the MCP server surface that Igris exposes through the product.
145.content: MCP Server What The MCP Server Is For Customer Contract Request Shape Core Method Families Integration Guidance Related Guides # MCP Server This page documents the MCP server surface that Igris exposes through the product. Treat MCP as part of the product contract rather than as a generic tool-call side channel. --- ## What The MCP Server Is For Use the MCP server when context needs to move between agents, tools, sessions, or runtimes in a structured way. That makes it useful for: - shared mission state - tool-oriented working context - multi-agent coordination - runtime-local or cross-runtime context exchange If the problem is only one request deep, keep the data in the request instead. Use MCP when the context belongs to the operating environment. ## Customer Contract The customer-facing hosted entry points are: - `POST /v1/mcp` for request/response JSON-RPC calls - `POST /v1/mcp/stream` for streaming MCP interactions The product forwards those calls to the appropriate runtime MCP server where needed, so the customer can keep thinking in terms of one product surface. ## Request Shape The MCP request body follows JSON-RPC 2.0: json { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "context/write", "params": { "key": "mission_state", "value": { "step": 3, "status": "navigating" } }, "id": 1 } ## Core Method Families The main MCP method families exposed through Igris today are: - `context/*` for structured shared context - `tools/*` for tool discovery and invocation Treat the specific method contract as part of your application integration, not as an undocumented side channel. ## Integration Guidance - keep request-local prompt data out of MCP unless it truly belongs in shared state - prefer explicit keys and schemas for shared context - do not mix audit evidence with working context - use durable tasks when progress recovery matters more than context recall ## Related Guides - [MCP →](/docs/mcp) - [Context Engineering →](/docs/context-engineering) - [Hybrid Deployment Workflow →](/docs/hybrid-deployment-workflow)

146.title: MCP Swarm Mode
146.description: MCP Swarm Mode extends structured context across multiple runtimes on the same network.
146.content: MCP Swarm Mode What It Solves Operational Model Configuration Design Boundaries Common Mistakes Related Guides # MCP Swarm Mode MCP Swarm Mode extends structured context across multiple runtimes on the same network. Use it when context must move between devices or runtime instances without turning every exchange into an application-managed synchronization problem. --- ## What It Solves Swarm Mode is useful when: - multiple runtimes need the same operational context - one runtime should be able to continue after another runtime wrote the latest shared state - distributed planning or robotics coordination needs a shared context layer ## Operational Model In Swarm Mode: - runtimes discover peers - shared context is replicated across the swarm - reads can be served from a peer that did not originate the write That makes Swarm Mode a context-sharing mechanism, not a replacement for durable workflow recovery or audit evidence. ## Configuration toml [mcp_swarm] enabled = true discovery = "mdns" encryption_key_path = "/path/to/swarm.key" ## Design Boundaries Use Swarm Mode for shared operational state. Do not use it for: - signed audit records - long-term business data retention - progress recovery that should be modeled as a durable task ## Common Mistakes - treating swarm replication as if it were a durable checkpoint protocol - storing too much request-local prompt state in the shared swarm context - using swarm state where one runtime-local value would be simpler ## Related Guides - [MCP →](/docs/mcp) - [MCP Server →](/docs/mcp-server) - [Context Engineering →](/docs/context-engineering)

147.title: Memory
147.description: Igris supports three memory systems: vector store for semantic retrieval, KV cache for fast key-value lookup, and cross-instance context via MCP Swarm Mode.
147.content: Memory Vector Store KV Cache Cross-Instance Context (MCP Swarm Mode) Agent Blackboard API GET /v1/agents/memory/ GET /v1/agents/memory/:key PUT /v1/agents/memory/:key DELETE /v1/agents/memory/:key → 204 No Content On-Device Training # Memory Igris supports three memory systems: vector store for semantic retrieval, KV cache for fast key-value lookup, and cross-instance context via MCP Swarm Mode. --- ## Vector Store The vector store indexes embeddings and retrieves semantically similar documents at query time. It gives agents access to a long-term knowledge base without including everything in the context window. **How it works:** 1. Documents are embedded and stored in the local vector index 2. At query time, the agent provides a query string 3. The vector store returns the top-K most similar documents 4. Retrieved documents are injected into the agent's context **Configuration:** json { "memory": { "vector_store": { "enabled": true, "top_k": 5, "similarity_threshold": 0.75 } } } **Supported embedding models:** - Any GGUF-format embedding model - External embedding APIs (via the HTTP tool) The vector index is stored on device. Embeddings do not leave the device unless you configure an external embedding endpoint. --- ## KV Cache The KV cache provides fast key-value storage for agent state that must persist across steps or across executions. **Use cases:** - Storing intermediate results between planning steps - Persisting agent state across tool calls - Caching frequently accessed data to reduce tool call latency **Access:** json { "kv_cache": { "set": }, "get": , "ttl_seconds": 3600 } } KV entries expire after `ttl_seconds`. The cache is local to the engine instance unless MCP Swarm Mode is enabled. --- ## Cross-Instance Context (MCP Swarm Mode) MCP Swarm Mode enables execution context to be shared across multiple engine instances. Any instance in the swarm can access context written by another instance. **How it works:** - Instances auto-discover each other via mDNS on the local network - Context is written to shared encrypted storage (AES-256-GCM) - Any instance can read context written by any other instance - Context is available within milliseconds of being written **Use cases:** - Multi-robot coordination: one robot updates mission state, others read it - High-availability: if one instance goes offline, another continues the execution - Distributed agents: agents on different nodes share a working memory **Configuration:** json { "mcp_swarm": { "enabled": true, "discovery": "mdns", "encryption_key_path": "/path/to/swarm.key" } } The encryption key is device-specific and must be dis

148.title: Model Aggregation
148.description: > Infinite Tier — Federated model aggregation is included with the Infinite plan.
148.content: Model Aggregation What It Is Architecture Aggregation Rounds Round Configuration Privacy API GET /v1/federated/status GET /v1/federated/participants GET /v1/federated/rounds POST /v1/federated/rounds/start GET /v1/federated/config PUT /v1/federated/config Console # Model Aggregation > **Infinite Tier** — Federated model aggregation is included with the Infinite plan. Igris supports federated learning across your fleet of Runtime devices, enabling collaborative model improvement without sharing raw data between devices. --- ## What It Is Model Aggregation (federated learning) allows multiple Runtime devices to train local model updates (LoRA adapters) and aggregate them into a global model improvement — all without sending training data off-device. Device A: trains local adapter ──┐ Device B: trains local adapter ──┼──► Aggregator → Global model update Device C: trains local adapter ──┘ Each device: 1. Trains a LoRA adapter on its local execution history 2. Sends only the adapter weights (encrypted) to the aggregator 3. Receives the aggregated global model update 4. Applies the update to its local model Raw execution data never leaves the device. --- ## Architecture ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Coordination Layer (Cloud) │ │ │ │ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ Federated Coordinator │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ Round Manager → Aggregator → Model Distributor│ │ │ └──────────────────┬──────────────────────────┘ │ └─────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┘ │ ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐ │ │ │ ┌────▼────┐ ┌────▼────┐ ┌────▼────┐ │Device A │ │Device B │ │Device C │ │(LoRA) │ │(LoRA) │ │(LoRA) │ └─────────┘ └─────────┘ └─────────┘ --- ## Aggregation Rounds Federated learning operates in rounds: 1. **Round Start** — The coordinator triggers a new aggregation round 2. **Local Training** — Each participating device trains its LoRA adapter 3. **Weight Upload** — Devices upload encrypted adapter weights 4. **Aggregation** — The coordinator computes a weighted average of all adapters 5. **Distribution** — The aggregated model is sent back to all participants 6. **Application** — Each device loads the updated model ### Round Configuration json { "federated_learning": { "enabled": true, "min_participants": 3, "round_interval_mins": 60, "max_rounds_per_day": 12, "privacy_budget": 1.0, "noise_scale": 0.1 } } | Field | Type | Default | Description | |---|---|---|---| | `enabled` | bool | `false` | Enable federated learning | | `min_participants` | int | 3 | Minimum devices required to start a round | | `round_interval_mins` | int | 60 | Time between aggregation rounds | | `max_rounds_p

149.title: Multi-Tenancy
149.description: Igris supports multi-tenant deployments where a single infrastructure serves multiple isolated tenants. Each tenant has its own execution space, policies, keys, and audit trail.
149.content: Multi-Tenancy Architecture Isolation guarantees Tenant Identification Tenant Configuration Resource Quotas Cross-Tenant Isolation Data isolation Network isolation Key isolation Billing # Multi-Tenancy Igris supports multi-tenant deployments where a single infrastructure serves multiple isolated tenants. Each tenant has its own execution space, policies, keys, and audit trail. --- ## Architecture Multi-tenancy in Igris is enforced at every layer: ┌─────────────────────────┐ │ Coordination Layer │ │ │ │ Tenant A │ Tenant B │ │ Tenant C │ Tenant D │ └────────┬────────────────┘ │ ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐ │ │ │ ┌─────┴─────┐ ┌─────┴─────┐ ┌─────┴─────┐ │ Runtime A │ │ Runtime B │ │ Runtime C │ │ (Tenant A) │ │ (Tenant B) │ │ (Tenant C) │ └───────────┘ └───────────┘ └───────────┘ ### Isolation guarantees | Layer | Isolation method | |---|---| | **Inference** | Separate API keys, separate provider configurations | | **Execution** | Separate execution envelopes with tenant-scoped IDs | | **Data** | Tenant-scoped storage — no cross-tenant data access | | **Policies** | Per-tenant policy envelopes | | **Audit** | Per-tenant receipt chains | | **Keys** | Per-tenant vault — keys are never shared | --- ## Tenant Identification Every request is associated with a tenant via the API key used for authentication. The API key maps to exactly one tenant. There is no cross-tenant key. API Key → Tenant ID → Execution Context The tenant ID is embedded in every execution receipt, ensuring full traceability from receipt back to tenant. --- ## Tenant Configuration Each tenant has an independent configuration: json { "tenant": { "id": "tenant-abc123", "name": "Acme Corp", "tier": "horizon", "providers": ["anthropic", "openai"], "policy": { "max_tokens": 4096, "max_steps": 10, "allow_http": true, "allow_shell": false }, "slo": { "latency_p99_ms": 2000, "max_cost_per_request_usd": 0.05 } } } --- ## Resource Quotas Tenants are allocated resource quotas based on their tier: | Resource | Seed | Horizon | Infinite | |---|---|---|---| | Runtime instances | 3 | 50 | 500 | | Receipt retention | 7 days | 30 days | 90 days | | Federated learning | — | — | ✓ | | SLO enforcement | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | | Routing advisor | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | When a tenant exceeds its quota, requests are rejected with HTTP 429. The `X-RateLimit-Remaining` header indicates remaining capacity. --- ## Cross-Tenant Isolation ### Data isolation - Execution receipts are scoped to tenant — no tenant can query another tenant's receipts - Vector store indexes are tenant-scoped - KV cache entries are tenant-scoped -

150.title: Multimodal Inference
150.description: > Early Access — Multimodal inference is currently in early access. The API is functional but subject to change. Contact support@igrisinertial.com to enable it for your account.
150.content: Multimodal Inference POST /v1/infer/multimodal GET /v1/infer/multimodal/stats Supported providers # Multimodal Inference > **Early Access** — Multimodal inference is currently in early access. The API is functional but subject to change. Contact [support@igrisinertial.com](mailto:support@igrisinertial.com) to enable it for your account. Igris supports multimodal inference — requests that include text plus image or audio inputs. The coordination layer routes multimodal requests to providers that support the requested modalities. --- ## POST /v1/infer/multimodal Send a prompt alongside image or audio data. The request is routed to a provider with multimodal capability. bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/infer/multimodal \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "prompt": "Describe what you see in this image.", "image_data": " " }' **Request fields:** <TypeTable type={{ prompt: { type: 'string', description: 'Text prompt sent alongside image or audio inputs.', required: true, }, image_data: { type: 'string', description: 'Base64-encoded image payload. Supports JPEG, PNG, and WebP.', }, audio_data: { type: 'string', description: 'Base64-encoded audio payload. Supports MP3, WAV, and M4A.', }, }} /> At least one of `image_data` or `audio_data` must be provided alongside `prompt`. **Response:** json { "content": "The image shows a robotic arm in a warehouse environment...", "input_tokens": 142, "output_tokens": 87, "latency_ms": 1240, "modalities": ["text", "image"] } <TypeTable type={{ content: { type: 'string', description: 'Model response text.', required: true, }, input_tokens: { type: 'number', description: 'Tokens consumed by text and multimodal encoding.', required: true, }, output_tokens: { type: 'number', description: 'Tokens emitted in the response.', required: true, }, latency_ms: { type: 'number', description: 'End-to-end request latency in milliseconds.', required: true, }, modalities: { type: 'Array ', description: 'Modalities used in this request.', required: true, }, }} /> --- ## GET /v1/infer/multimodal/stats Usage analytics for multimodal inference. bash curl https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/infer/multimodal/stats \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" Response: json { "total_requests": 2841, "image_requests": 2503, "audio_requests": 338, "avg_latency_ms": 1187.4 } --- ## Supported providers | Provider | Image | Audio | |---|---|---| | OpenAI (GPT-4V, GPT-4o) | ✓ | ✓ |

151.title: Observability & Tracing
151.description: How Igris exposes request lineage, trace IDs, and distributed tracing across the coordination layer and runtime.
151.content: Observability & Tracing Trace Identity Distributed Tracing What Operators Should Expect Relationship To Receipts Recommended Deployment Model Related Pages # Observability & Tracing Igris has two observability layers: - **product-visible lineage** such as request IDs, receipts, and execution history - **operator-visible tracing** such as spans, trace propagation, and deployment telemetry You need both. Receipts tell you what happened. Tracing tells you where time was spent and where a request crossed system boundaries. --- ## Trace Identity The coordination layer generates and propagates a trace identity for each request. That identity is attached to logs and returned through `X-Trace-ID` so operators can correlate: - inbound API traffic - routing decisions - provider calls - runtime handoff - receipt and audit records From a product perspective, `X-Trace-ID` is the fast path for debugging cross-system behavior. --- ## Distributed Tracing Igris supports OpenTelemetry-style tracing with a Jaeger exporter and request-scoped trace attributes. That combination matters because Igris needs to support both: - cross-service span propagation - external tracing systems used by platform teams Current tracing metadata includes things like: - HTTP method and path - provider and model - token counts - latency and cost - speculative-execution winner and switch metadata This makes tracing useful for routing analysis, not just generic HTTP timing. --- ## What Operators Should Expect Tracing should answer these questions quickly: - Did the request stay in cloud or move to runtime? - Which provider was selected and why? - Where did latency accumulate? - Was speculative execution involved? - Is a slow request caused by routing, provider latency, or local runtime work? That is the difference between basic logging and a usable production observability model. --- ## Relationship To Receipts Tracing and receipts are related but not interchangeable. | Surface | Primary use | |---|---| | **Trace ID / spans** | live debugging, latency analysis, request-path inspection | | **Execution receipt** | tamper-evident record of the governed execution outcome | Use tracing when you are diagnosing behavior in-flight. Use receipts when you need durable audit evidence. --- ## Recommended Deployment Model For production environments: - return or capture `X-Trace-ID` in client and operator tooling - export traces to your tracing system - correlate traces with execution receipts and request IDs - retain tracing for operations and receipts for governanc

154.title: Provider Health
154.description: Igris continuously monitors the health of your configured AI providers and uses this data to make intelligent routing decisions.
154.content: Provider Health Health Metrics Health Status Levels Active Degraded Unavailable Health Monitoring Pipeline Provider Health Dashboard Health API GET /v1/providers/stats GET /v1/providers/:id/health Automatic Actions Health Checks # Provider Health Igris continuously monitors the health of your configured AI providers and uses this data to make intelligent routing decisions. --- ## Health Metrics For each provider, Igris tracks: | Metric | Description | |---|---| | **Status** | `active`, `degraded`, or `unavailable` | | **Latency (p50)** | Median response time over the last 5 minutes | | **Latency (p99)** | 99th percentile response time over the last 5 minutes | | **Success rate** | Percentage of successful requests in the last 5 minutes | | **Error rate** | Percentage of failed requests in the last 5 minutes | | **Requests/min** | Current throughput | | **Cost/request** | Average cost per request in USD | --- ## Health Status Levels ### Active The provider is operating normally: - Success rate ≥ 95% - p99 latency within SLO target - Circuit breaker is closed ### Degraded The provider is experiencing issues but still functional: - Success rate between 80% and 95% - p99 latency elevated but within 2× SLO target - Circuit breaker may be half-open ### Unavailable The provider is not usable: - Success rate < 80% - p99 latency exceeds 2× SLO target - Circuit breaker is open --- ## Health Monitoring Pipeline Provider Response → Metrics Collector → Health Evaluator → Routing Decision 1. **Metrics Collector** — records latency, success/failure, and cost for every request 2. **Health Evaluator** — computes rolling averages and determines health status 3. **Routing Decision** — The routing engine uses health data to select the best provider The health evaluation runs on a sliding window (default 5 minutes). Older data decays exponentially. --- ## Provider Health Dashboard View provider health in the Console at `/models/providers`: - **Provider cards** — status badge, latency, success rate, and last checked time - **Latency chart** — p50 and p99 latency over the last 24 hours - **Success rate chart** — rolling success rate over the last 24 hours - **Cost chart** — average cost per request over time --- ## Health API ### GET /v1/providers/stats Returns health and performance statistics for all configured providers. bash curl https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/providers/stats \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" Response: json { "providers": [ { "name": "anthropic", "status": "active", "latency_p50_ms": 287, "latency_p99_ms": 512, "success_rate": 0.994, "error_rate": 0.006, "requests_per_m

155.title: Provider Trust
155.description: How Igris scores whether a provider should still be trusted for routing based on observed behavior instead of provider claims alone.
155.content: Provider Trust What Trust Measures Fail-Closed Behavior Cold Start And Confidence Divergence And Decay How It Affects Routing What To Document For Operators Related Pages # Provider Trust Provider health and provider trust are not the same thing. - **Health** asks whether a provider is up right now. - **Trust** asks whether the provider is behaving close enough to what it claims that Igris should keep routing traffic there. This distinction matters in production. --- ## What Trust Measures The trust model compares **observed behavior** against **reported or expected behavior**. Current trust inputs include: - observed latency - observed error rate - observed cost - divergence from reported latency, error rate, and cost - confidence level based on sample count That lets the router react not only to outages, but also to providers that quietly drift away from their stated performance envelope. --- ## Fail-Closed Behavior Provider trust is intentionally fail-closed. A provider can be blocked when: - the trust score drops below the configured threshold - there are not enough samples to trust the provider yet - the provider is unknown to the trust tracker That is stricter than ordinary health monitoring, and it should be understood as part of Igris's safety posture. --- ## Cold Start And Confidence Trust is not binary. It grows with evidence. New or rarely used providers start with low confidence. In the current model, sample count determines when trust becomes stable enough for normal routing decisions. This protects the system from treating an unverified provider as production-ready just because it responded once. Operationally, that means provider onboarding has a warm-up phase. --- ## Divergence And Decay Trust decays when observed behavior diverges too far from reported behavior. Examples: - latency is materially worse than claimed - error rate is higher than expected - real cost is above the advertised envelope Trust can also decay over time without fresh activity. This prevents stale historical success from granting indefinite routing privilege. --- ## How It Affects Routing Provider trust sits in front of final provider selection. The decision stack is effectively: 1. Is the provider allowed by policy? 2. Is it healthy enough to consider? 3. Is it trusted enough to consider? 4. If yes, how should it be weighted against the alternatives? That means a provider can appear technically available while still being excluded from routing for trust reasons. --- ## What To Document For Operators Teams operating Igris should understan

156.description: Choose the simplest path that matches how you plan to run Igris.
156.content: Quick Start Prerequisites Option A: Cloud API 1. Add a provider key 2. Point your client at Igris Option B: Local Runtime 1. Download the runtime archive 2. Extract and install 3. Start the runtime with registration credentials 2. Use the cloud API from your application What To Do Next Troubleshooting # Quick Start Choose the simplest path that matches how you plan to run Igris. If you are unsure where to begin, start with the hosted OpenAI-compatible API. It is the shortest path to a working production integration and the easiest path to validate product fit. Move to a native SDK when you need Igris-specific product features, and move to local runtime or hybrid deployment only when the workload truly needs on-device execution, fleet participation, or offline behavior. --- ## Prerequisites - An Igris account at [console.igrisinertial.com](https://console.igrisinertial.com) - One tenant API key (`igris_...`) from **Settings → API Keys** - For cloud routing today, provider keys for the currently supported public vault identifiers: `openai` or `anthropic` - For local runtime, a GGUF model file if you want on-device inference --- ## Option A: Cloud API This is the recommended starting path for most customers. 157.title: Rate Limiting
157.description: The hosted API applies a global rate limit of 100 requests per minute by default. Runtime binary downloads also have a dedicated 10 downloads per hour per tenant cap.
157.content: Rate Limiting What The Hosted API Enforces 429 Response Shape Runtime Download Limit Local Runtime Rate Limits Client Guidance # Rate Limiting The hosted API applies a global rate limit of **100 requests per minute** by default. Runtime binary downloads also have a dedicated **10 downloads per hour per tenant** cap. --- ## What The Hosted API Enforces The hosted API applies: - one shared window: `100 req/min` by default - scoped per tenant when tenant context exists, otherwise per IP The hosted API does **not** publish rate-limit headers on every successful response. Rate-limit headers are guaranteed on rejection responses. --- ## 429 Response Shape When the global limiter is exceeded, the current response looks like this: json { "error": { "message": "Rate limit exceeded. Please try again later.", "type": "rate_limit_error", "code": "RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED" }, "retry_after_seconds": 60 } Headers on the rejection path include: - `Retry-After` - `X-RateLimit-Limit` - `X-RateLimit-Remaining` Do not depend on `X-RateLimit-Reset` being present on successful requests in the current build. --- ## Runtime Download Limit Runtime archive downloads have a separate limit of `10/hour` per tenant on the control plane download surface. This applies to: - `GET /v1/runtime/download` - subscribed runtime download workflows behind the cloud control plane --- ## Local Runtime Rate Limits The local runtime auth config supports its own request controls: json5 { auth: { enabled: true, api_key: "YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY", rate_limit_per_minute: 60, rate_limit_burst: 10 } } | Field | Description | |---|---| | `rate_limit_per_minute` | Maximum local requests per minute | | `rate_limit_burst` | Additional local burst budget | --- ## Client Guidance - Treat `429` plus `retry_after_seconds` as the contract - Add exponential backoff client-side - Batch receipt exports and large history queries - Do not assume tier-specific global limits unless they are explicitly published in a future release contract --- [Troubleshooting →](/docs/troubleshooting) · [API Reference →](/docs/api-reference)

158.title: Receipts and Audit Workflow
158.description: Use this workflow when you need verifiable execution history, exportable receipts, or customer-visible audit evidence.
158.content: Receipts and Audit Workflow 1. Run requests through the documented product surface 2. Query recent execution history 3. Retrieve receipts for audit evidence 4. Export receipts for downstream systems 5. Verify before external use Common Mistakes Related Guides # Receipts and Audit Workflow Use this workflow when you need verifiable execution history, exportable receipts, or customer-visible audit evidence. This is the right path when you need to answer questions like: - what happened - what proof exists - what should be exported - what should be verified before it leaves the product boundary --- ## 1. Run requests through the documented product surface Receipts are most useful when traffic is consistently going through the intended Igris contract. Keep integrations on documented API paths so receipts, history, and exports line up with real product behavior instead of ad hoc side paths. ## 2. Query recent execution history Use execution history when you want a timeline view of what happened: - [API Reference →](/docs/api-reference) History is useful for dashboards and investigations. It tells you what happened over time. It is not the same thing as a proof artifact. ## 3. Retrieve receipts for audit evidence Use receipt listing and detail endpoints when you need the signed or hash-linked execution record itself. This is the surface you should treat as the audit artifact, not the history stream. - [Execution Receipts →](/docs/execution-receipts) - [API Reference →](/docs/api-reference) ## 4. Export receipts for downstream systems Use `GET /v1/receipts/export` when you need to move receipt data into BI, compliance, or external archive systems. Choose NDJSON for machine pipelines and CSV for spreadsheet-oriented workflows. ## 5. Verify before external use If a workflow depends on the integrity of a receipt, verify it before using it as an external audit artifact. Verification should happen before the receipt is relied on by another system, reviewer, or compliance process. ## Common Mistakes - Treating execution history as if it were the same thing as the signed receipt - Exporting receipts without deciding on a durable downstream retention model - Skipping verification when the receipt is leaving the product boundary ## Related Guides - [Execution Receipts →](/docs/execution-receipts) - [Audit →](/docs/audit) - [API Errors →](/docs/api-reference/errors)

159.content: Robotics Deployment on Robotics Hardware ROS2 Integration Mission Execution Safety in Robotics Fleet Management # Robotics Igris runs on robotics hardware with native ROS2 integration, fleet coordination, and mission execution governance. The same execution model — bounded envelopes, signed receipts — applies to robotic agents. --- ## Deployment on Robotics Hardware The execution engine runs on embedded and robotics hardware: | Platform | Architecture | Notes | |---|---|---| | Raspberry Pi 4/5 | ARM64 | Edge inference | | NVIDIA Jetson | ARM64 | GPU-accelerated inference | | x86 industrial PC | x86_64 | Full-size deployment | On ARM64 hardware without a GPU, Phi-3 Mini runs comfortably at 2–4 tokens/second. For time-sensitive control loops, configure the engine to use local inference exclusively and eliminate network latency. --- ## ROS2 Integration Igris exposes a ROS2 bridge that publishes and subscribes to ROS topics. AI agents can read sensor data from ROS topics and publish decisions back to the ROS graph. **Supported ROS2 distributions:** Humble, Iron, Jazzy **Configuration:** yaml ros2: enabled: true namespace: /igris input_topics: - /camera/image_raw - /lidar/scan - /odom output_topics: - /cmd_vel - /mission_status The ROS2 bridge is governed by the same capability model as other tool use. Publish operations require `tool_ros2_publish` capability grant. Subscribe operations are read-only and require no grant. [ROS2 Integration →](/docs/ros2-integration) --- ## Mission Execution Igris uses behavior trees to structure robotic missions. A behavior tree defines the mission as a hierarchy of conditions and actions. The execution engine traverses the tree, invoking AI agents at decision nodes. **Example mission structure:** Navigate to waypoint ├── [Condition: path clear?] │ ├── [Success] → Move to waypoint │ └── [Failure] → Replan path │ └── [AI agent: generate alternate route] └── [Condition: obstacle detected?] └── [Success] → Emergency stop Behavior trees run inside the execution envelope. Each tick of the tree consumes from `max_steps`. If the tree exhausts its step budget, the mission is terminated gracefully and the receipt records the state at termination. [Behavior Trees →](/docs/behavior-trees) --- ## Safety in Robotics For physical safety in robotics deployments, Igris provides: **Execution time limits.** Missions are bounded by `max_duration_ms`. 161.title: Safety & Containment
161.description: Igris enforces safety limits at the execution engine level — not at the application layer, where they could be bypassed.
161.content: Safety & Containment Containment Model Resource limits cgroup bounds (Linux) Capability Enforcement Secure Defaults Violation Handling Human-in-the-Loop # Safety & Containment Igris enforces safety limits at the execution engine level — not at the application layer, where they could be bypassed. --- ## Containment Model Every execution runs in a containment context. The containment context applies resource limits before the model is invoked and enforces them throughout execution. ### Resource limits Limits are applied per-execution: | Limit | Default | Description | |---|---|---| | `max_tokens` | 4096 | Maximum output tokens | | `max_duration_ms` | 30000 | Maximum wall time (30s) | | `max_steps` | 10 | Maximum tool/planning steps | | `max_tool_calls` | 5 | Maximum tool invocations per execution | Limits can be tightened per-tenant or per-request. They cannot be relaxed beyond the configured policy maximum. ### cgroup bounds (Linux) On Linux deployments, the engine applies cgroup constraints to the execution process: - **CPU quota**: limits CPU burst during local model inference - **Memory limit**: prevents unbounded memory growth in local inference - **I/O limits**: optional disk I/O rate limits for file-system tool use cgroup enforcement is independent of application code. An agent that attempts to consume more resources than its cgroup allows is throttled or killed by the kernel. --- ## Capability Enforcement Capabilities are enforced by the engine, not by the model. Even if the model generates output that attempts a disallowed tool call, the engine intercepts and rejects it before the call executes. The enforcement sequence: 1. Request arrives with a capability grant (or secure defaults are applied) 2. Engine validates the grant against the tenant's policy ceiling 3. Engine begins execution with the validated grant in scope 4. If the model attempts a tool call, the engine checks the grant before executing 5. If the call is outside the grant, the engine records a capability violation and rejects the call 6. Execution continues or terminates depending on the violation policy Violation events are recorded in the execution receipt. They cannot be suppressed. --- ## Secure Defaults The engine applies secure defaults when capability grants are not explicitly specified: | Setting | Default | |---|---| | `allow_http` | disabled | | `allow_shell` | disabled | | `allow_filesystem` | disabled | | `max_tokens` | 2048 | | `max_steps` | 5 | Tools must be explicitly enabled. The defaults assume no tool use is intended.

162.content: SDKs Support Matrix Support Policy OpenAI-Compatible Clients Native SDKs JavaScript / TypeScript Go Rust Python Store a provider API key List registered fleet agents Deployment Mode Guidance Request Contract Code Quality Expectations # SDKs Igris supports two integration paths: - **OpenAI-compatible clients** for the fastest path to production - **Native Igris SDKs** when you need routing metadata, receipt helpers, vault operations, fleet APIs, behavior trees, or containment The recommendation is simple: - Start with the OpenAI-compatible API if you want the shortest path to a working integration - Move to a native SDK when you need Igris-specific product features and a stronger typed client The native first-class SDKs are JavaScript/TypeScript, Go, Rust, and Python. Java, C#, and Ruby should use the OpenAI-compatible API today. For production integration guidance, reusable client construction, and environment-variable patterns, continue with [SDK Integration Patterns →](/docs/sdk-integration-patterns). ## Support Matrix ## Support Policy Treat the SDK table as a product support statement, not just a package list: - **First-class** means the language is part of the maintained customer SDK surface - **OpenAI-compatible** means the safest contract today is the HTTP API through an OpenAI-style client If your team wants the strongest support commitment, choose JavaScript/TypeScript, Go, Rust, or Python. If your team mainly needs inference and broad portability, stay on the OpenAI-compatible path. --- ## OpenAI-Compatible Clients Any OpenAI SDK can call Igris by changing the base URL. For many teams, this is the right default because it keeps the integration portable while still routing through the product. **Python** python import os from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI( base_url="https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1", api_key=os.environ["IGRIS_API_KEY"], ) response = client.chat.completions.create( model="gpt-4", messages=[ ], ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) **JavaScript / TypeScript** typescript const client = new OpenAI({ baseURL: 'https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1', apiKey: process.env.IGRIS_API_KEY, }); const response = await client.chat.completions.create({ model: 'gpt-4', messages: [ ], }); console.log(response.choices[0].message.content); Use this path for Java, C#, Ruby, or any other language where you already have an OpenAI-compatible client and do not need the native Igris SDK surface yet. --- ## Native SDKs Choose a native SDK when you want a product-shaped client rather than a protocol-shaped one. That matters when you are working with receipts, vault oper JavaScript / TypeScript first-class Preferred native SDK for browser and Node.js integrations. Go first-class Preferred native SDK for backend services and CLI tooling. Rust first-class Preferred native SDK for systems and embedded integrations. Python first-class Preferred native SDK for Python services, data pipelines, and scripting. Java openai-compatible Use the OpenAI-compatible API until a native Java SDK is promoted explicitly. C# openai-compatible Use the OpenAI-compatible API until a native C# SDK is promoted explicitly. Ruby openai-compatible Use the OpenAI-compatible API until a native Ruby SDK is promoted explicitly.

163.title: SDK Integration Patterns
163.description: This guide shows how to use the SDK surface in a way that is maintainable in production.
163.content: SDK Integration Patterns Choose The Right Client Surface First Standard Environment Variables Pattern: Choose A Mode Once Pattern: Centralize Client Construction JavaScript / TypeScript Go Rust Pattern: Separate Hosted And Local Modes Cleanly JavaScript / TypeScript mode switch Pattern: Handle Product Errors Explicitly Pattern: Keep Receipt And Audit Handling Out Of The Hot Path Pattern: Start Portable, Then Go Deeper Production Checklist Related Guides # SDK Integration Patterns This guide shows how to use the SDK surface in a way that is maintainable in production. It is not a language feature catalog. It is the set of patterns that keep integrations clean when the same product may be called in cloud, local-runtime, or hybrid deployments. --- ## Choose The Right Client Surface First Start with this decision: - Use an OpenAI-compatible client when you want the shortest path to a working integration - Use a native Igris SDK when you need product-specific features such as receipts, vault operations, fleet controls, or richer routing metadata The first-class native SDKs today are: - JavaScript / TypeScript - Go - Rust - Python If you are in Java, C#, Ruby, or another language without a first-class native SDK, the safest default is still the OpenAI-compatible API. ## Standard Environment Variables Use the same environment-variable model across languages: - `IGRIS_API_KEY` for hosted API access - `IGRIS_BASE_URL` when you need to override the default base URL Recommended defaults: - hosted API: `https://overture.igrisinertial.com` - local runtime: `http://localhost:8080` Keeping this consistent is one of the easiest ways to make cloud, local, and hybrid deployments feel like one product to your own application teams. ## Pattern: Choose A Mode Once Do not let every handler decide whether it is in cloud, local, or hybrid mode. Make that a startup concern: - cloud mode points to `https://overture.igrisinertial.com` - local mode points to `http://localhost:8080` - hybrid mode usually still keeps application traffic on the hosted API, while Igris coordinates work with runtimes behind that surface The goal is to keep your business logic unaware of deployment details whenever possible. ## Pattern: Centralize Client Construction Do not scatter client creation across handlers and jobs. Create one small constructor per service and keep the auth/base-URL decision there. ### JavaScript / TypeScript typescript export function createIgrisClient() { const apiKey = process.env.IGRIS_API_KEY; if (!apiKey) { throw new Error('IGRIS_API_KEY is required'); } return new IgrisClient({ baseUrl: process.env.IGRIS_BASE_URL ?? 164.title: Security
164.description: Igris security has two distinct planes:
164.content: Security Authentication Tenant API Keys Console Sessions Provider Keys Policy And Capability Controls Receipts And Verification Deployment Notes Compliance # Security Igris security has two distinct planes: - **Tenant API keys** for automation and programmatic access - **Console session cookies** for browser access to the web app Treat those as different contracts. --- ## Authentication ### Tenant API Keys Tenant API keys use the `igris_` prefix and are accepted in: - `Authorization: Bearer YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY` - `X-API-Key: YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY` Best practices: - Store tenant API keys in environment variables - Rotate them if exposed - Scope usage to the tenant that owns the key bash export IGRIS_API_KEY="igris_abc123..." ### Console Sessions The web console uses Better Auth session cookies. Those cookies are not a published bearer-token contract. Do not script console session access as generic bearer authorization headers. ### Provider Keys Provider keys stored through the current public vault API are encrypted before storage and returned only as masked values. --- ## Policy And Capability Controls A restrictive starting point in the current control-plane policy model looks like this: json { "allow_http": false, "allow_shell": false, "allow_fs_write": false, "allow_external_api": false, "domain_allowlist": [], "domain_denylist": [], "writable_paths": [], "readable_paths": [], "violation_behavior": "terminate" } Start tight, then expand based on observed violations and actual agent requirements. --- ## Receipts And Verification Customer-facing verification routes currently live on the proof API: - `GET /proof/receipts` - `POST /proof/receipts/verify` - `GET /v1/proof/violations` Example: bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/proof/receipts/verify \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d ' ' --- ## Deployment Notes - The local runtime can enforce its own API key with the local `auth` config - Fleet registration is gated by a valid `IGRIS_LICENSE_KEY` plus `IGRIS_API_KEY` - For local-only deployments, point clients directly at the runtime and keep your own storage if you need offline receipt retention --- ## Compliance Igris is positioned to support compliance workflows, but the exact operational model depends on where you run the control plane and runtime. - **Data residency** depends on whether you call Overture, the local runtime, or both - **Auditability** comes from receipts, proof endpoints, and export workflows - **Least privilege** comes from capabi

165.title: Semantic Routing
165.description: How Igris classifies prompts before provider selection so routing decisions can adapt to workload type rather than raw provider averages alone.
165.content: Semantic Routing Why It Exists Decision Flow Fallback Behavior What Gets Learned Operational Implications Where It Fits Related Pages # Semantic Routing Igris does not have to treat every prompt as the same workload. Semantic routing adds a classification step before provider selection so the router can make different decisions for different classes of work. Examples: - code generation - extraction or structured tasks - general reasoning - default fallback traffic when classification is unavailable --- ## Why It Exists A provider that performs well for one workload may not be the best choice for another. Global averages hide that. Semantic routing improves this by combining: - **prompt classification** - **provider capability filtering** - **per-class reward tracking** - **Thompson-sampling exploration and exploitation** The result is a router that can prefer different providers for different prompt classes without hard-coding static rules for every workload. --- ## Decision Flow Prompt -> Semantic classifier -> Workload class -> Eligible providers -> Thompson sampling -> Selected provider The routing flow behaves like this: 1. Classify the incoming prompt with a short timeout. 2. Convert the class into a required capability or provider slice. 3. Remove unhealthy candidates. 4. Select among the remaining candidates using per-class bandit arms. 5. Record feedback from the real request outcome. That is materially different from simple round-robin or provider-weight routing. --- ## Fallback Behavior Semantic routing is intentionally not a hard dependency. If the classifier is disabled or classification fails, Igris falls back to regular Thompson-sampling routing instead of failing the request. That matters operationally because it keeps routing availability higher than classifier availability. In other words: - classification success improves decision quality - classification failure should not become an outage --- ## What Gets Learned The router tracks reward per provider and per semantic class. In practice, that lets Igris learn things like: - one provider is stronger for code-heavy prompts - another is cheaper for default chat traffic - a provider should be explored less for a class where it underperforms This is one reason routing behavior can change over time even when your fallback chain stays the same. --- ## Operational Implications Semantic routing should be operated as an explicit product capability. Teams should expect: - class-specific routing behavior - class-specific performance

166.title: Shadow Mode
166.description: Shadow Mode runs a parallel execution alongside your real execution, using a different provider or configuration, without affecting the actual output. It lets you compare providers
166.content: Shadow Mode How It Works Use Cases Provider Comparison Configuration Testing Quality Monitoring Configuration Shadow Comparison API GET /v1/execution/shadow Divergence Score Console Cost Considerations # Shadow Mode Shadow Mode runs a parallel execution alongside your real execution, using a different provider or configuration, without affecting the actual output. It lets you compare providers, test new configurations, and detect quality degradation — all in production with zero risk. --- ## How It Works When Shadow Mode is enabled for an agent: Request → Real Execution (enforced) ──► Response to caller ↘ Shadow Execution (observed) ──► Comparison stored 1. 168.description: How Igris evaluates runtime and routing health against latency, error-rate, availability, and throughput objectives, and what is customer-facing today.
168.content: SLO Enforcer What Is Enforced Evaluation Output Customer-Facing Surfaces Operational Access Integration Guidance # SLO Enforcer Igris uses SLO enforcement to keep routing and runtime execution inside operational bounds. The enforcer evaluates live metrics, classifies breaches, and produces remediation actions that the platform can execute or record. The current customer-facing contract is not a standalone SLO configuration API. Customers see SLO outcomes through routing behavior, provider health, execution receipts, history, and observability views. --- ## What Is Enforced The production enforcer evaluates these metric inputs: | Metric | Target | Warning | Critical | |---|---:|---:|---:| | `p99_latency_ms` | `100` | `130` | `150` | | `p95_latency_ms` | `50` | `80` | `100` | | `error_rate` | `0.001` | `0.01` | `0.02` | | `availability` | `0.9999` | `0.999` | `0.99` | | `throughput_rps` | `10000` | `8000` | `5000` | The enforcer is configured with a 20-second evaluation interval and a 300-second breach cooldown. Auto-remediation is enabled in the default production configuration. --- ## Evaluation Output SLO evaluations are exposed to customers through supported product surfaces rather than a standalone public SLO API. Use provider-health state, routing statistics, execution receipts, history, and observability exports to understand when the platform detected degraded behavior and how traffic was handled. --- ## Customer-Facing Surfaces Use these documented surfaces to understand SLO behavior: - [Provider Health](/docs/provider-health) for provider status and degradation signals. - [Circuit Breaker](/docs/circuit-breaker) for provider trip state and recovery behavior. - [Routing Control & Analytics](/docs/api-reference/routing-control-analytics/get-v1-routing-stats) for routing telemetry. - [Execution Receipts](/docs/execution-receipts) for receipt-level evidence that an execution completed, failed, or violated policy. - [Observability & Tracing](/docs/observability-tracing) for deployment-level monitoring. --- ## Operational Access SLO administration is not part of the public API reference. For enterprise deployments that require direct operational access, use the account-specific surfaces and runbooks provided with that deployment. --- ## Integration Guidance Do not build customer automation against standalone SLO configuration or compliance routes; they are not part of the current production API. For customer integrations: - Use routing and provider-health APIs to obs

169.title: Speculative Execution
169.description: Speculative execution runs a lightweight draft inference in parallel with the main inference. When the draft result meets a quality threshold, it is returned immediately — before t
169.content: Speculative Execution How It Works When It Helps When It Does Not Help Tier Availability Enabling Speculative Execution Enable for your tenant {"saved": true} Check current configuration Check live status Reading Analytics Simulating Before Enabling Interaction with Other Features # Speculative Execution Speculative execution runs a lightweight draft inference in parallel with the main inference. When the draft result meets a quality threshold, it is returned immediately — before the main inference completes. This reduces time-to-first-token by up to 60% for streaming requests, at no change to output quality for the workloads where it applies. --- ## How It Works When speculative execution is enabled, each incoming inference request spawns two parallel paths: 1. **Draft path** — A faster, smaller model generates a candidate response. The draft is evaluated for quality as it streams. 2. **Main path** — The configured primary model processes the request normally. If the draft meets the acceptance threshold before the main inference completes, the draft is returned immediately and the main inference is cancelled. If the draft does not meet the threshold — because the task is too complex or unpredictable for the draft model — the main inference result is returned instead. The caller always receives one response. The distinction between draft and main is not exposed in the response payload. The execution receipt records which path was used. --- ## When It Helps Speculative execution provides the most benefit in these scenarios: **Streaming responses with latency requirements.** The time-to-first-token improvement is most noticeable in streaming use cases where users are waiting for a response to begin. Draft acceptance reduces the delay before the first token arrives. **Repetitive or predictable completions.** Tasks like summarization, translation, structured data extraction, and templated generation tend to have high draft acceptance rates because the output space is constrained and the draft model handles them well. **High-throughput batch workloads where p50 latency is a key metric.** At scale, improving the median case across many requests compounds into a significant reduction in overall processing time. --- ## When It Does Not Help **Non-streaming requests.** For non-streaming calls, the latency benefit is smaller because the caller waits for the full response regardless. Speculative execution still applies, but the improvement to perceived latency is minimal. **Highly creative or open-ended tasks.** Tasks like long-form creative writing, complex multi-step reasoning, or novel problem-solving tend to have low draft acceptance rates —

170.content: Swarm & Council Mode Council Mode Enabling council mode per agent Configuring council mode → {"saved": true} Council analytics Cost considerations Swarm Mode GET /v1/fleet/swarm POST /v1/fleet/swarm/broadcast DELETE /v1/fleet/swarm/agents/:id/clear → {"cleared": true} Command Delivery # Swarm & Council Mode Igris supports two multi-agent coordination patterns: **Council Mode** for multi-provider consensus on a single request, and **Swarm Mode** for orchestrating commands across your entire fleet. --- ## Council Mode Council mode sends a request to multiple providers simultaneously and uses a chairman model to rank and synthesize the best response. Use it when response quality matters more than cost. ### Enabling council mode per agent bash curl -X PATCH https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/agents/agent-abc \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d ' ' ### Configuring council mode bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/routing/council \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "providers": ["anthropic", "openai", "google"], "chairman": "anthropic", "synthesis_strategy": "best_ranked" }' # → | Field | Description | |---|---| | `providers` | Providers to query in parallel | | `chairman` | Provider whose model ranks the responses | | `synthesis_strategy` | `best_ranked` returns the top-ranked response; `synthesize` asks the chairman to merge responses | ### Council analytics Query council round results: bash curl https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/routing/stats \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" Council metrics in the stats response show per-round cost, latency breakdown (ranking phase + synthesis phase), and winner distribution by provider. ### Cost considerations Council mode multiplies per-request cost by the number of providers queried. 171.title: Tamper-Evident Logs
171.description: Every execution in Igris produces a cryptographically signed receipt that forms part of an immutable audit trail. The tamper-evident log system ensures that no execution record can
171.content: Tamper-Evident Logs How It Works Chain Verification What's Recorded Export GET /v1/receipts/export Console Retention Audit Workflow # Tamper-Evident Logs Every execution in Igris produces a cryptographically signed receipt that forms part of an immutable audit trail. The tamper-evident log system ensures that no execution record can be altered, deleted, or inserted without detection. --- ## How It Works Each execution receipt contains: 1. **Envelope hash** — SHA-256 hash of the canonical execution envelope 2. **Previous hash** — SHA-256 hash of the previous receipt (forming a chain) 3. **Signature** — Ed25519 signature of the envelope using a device-bound key Each receipt links to the previous receipt via hash, forming a chain. Each receipt is signed with a device-bound key that exists only on the originating runtime. Tampering with any receipt invalidates its signature and breaks the chain — both of which are detected by the verification API. --- ## Chain Verification Receipts can be verified at any time to confirm chain integrity: bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/proof/receipts/verify \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d ' ' Response: json { "valid": true, "signature_valid": true, "chain_intact": true, "previous_hash_matches": true } If any link in the chain is broken, verification fails and the specific broken link is identified. --- ## What's Recorded Every receipt records: | Category | Fields | |---|---| | **Identity** | Request ID, tenant ID, agent ID, device ID, timestamp | | **Inputs** | Prompt, system message, parameters | | **Outputs** | Model response, tool call results | | **Resources** | Tokens consumed, wall time, CPU/memory usage | | **Capabilities** | Grants applied, violations recorded | | **Policy** | Policy hash at time of execution | | **Routing** | Provider selected, fallback count, latency | | **Chain** | Envelope hash, previous hash, signature | --- ## Export Receipts can be exported for external audit workflows: ### GET /v1/receipts/export Export receipts in the selected format and time range. bash curl "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/receipts/export?format=json&range=7d" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \ --output receipts_export.json Supported formats: - `json` — raw JSON array of receipts - `csv` — flattened CSV for spreadsheet analysis - `ndjson` — newline-delimited JSON for streaming processing --- ## Console View and verify receipts at `/proof/receipts`: - Receipt listing wit
