Igris supports federated learning across your fleet of Runtime devices, enabling collaborative model improvement without sharing raw data between devices. --- ## What It Is Model Aggregation (federated learning) allows multiple Runtime devices to train local model updates (LoRA adapters) and aggregate them into a global model improvement — all without sending training data off-device. Device A: trains local adapter ──┐ Device B: trains local adapter ──┼──► Aggregator → Global model update Device C: trains local adapter ──┘ Each device: 1. Trains a LoRA adapter on its local execution history 2. Sends only the adapter weights (encrypted) to the aggregator 3. Receives the aggregated global model update 4. Applies the update to its local model Raw execution data never leaves the device. --- ## Architecture ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Coordination Layer (Cloud) │ │ │ │ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ Federated Coordinator │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ Round Manager → Aggregator → Model Distributor│ │ │ └──────────────────┬──────────────────────────┘ │ └─────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┘ │ ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐ │ │ │ ┌────▼────┐ ┌────▼────┐ ┌────▼────┐ │Device A │ │Device B │ │Device C │ │(LoRA) │ │(LoRA) │ │(LoRA) │ └─────────┘ └─────────┘ └─────────┘ --- ## Aggregation Rounds Federated learning operates in rounds: 1. **Round Start** — The coordinator triggers a new aggregation round 2. **Local Training** — Each participating device trains its LoRA adapter 3. **Weight Upload** — Devices upload encrypted adapter weights 4. **Aggregation** — The coordinator computes a weighted average of all adapters 5. **Distribution** — The aggregated model is sent back to all participants 6. **Application** — Each device loads the updated model ### Round Configuration json { "federated_learning": { "enabled": true, "min_participants": 3, "round_interval_mins": 60, "max_rounds_per_day": 12, "privacy_budget": 1.0, "noise_scale": 0.1 } } | Field | Type | Default | Description | |---|---|---|---| | `enabled` | bool | `false` | Enable federated learning | | `min_participants` | int | 3 | Minimum devices required to start a round | | `round_interval_mins` | int | 60 | Time between aggregation rounds | | `max_rounds_p

Multi-Tenancy Architecture Isolation guarantees Tenant Identification Tenant Configuration Resource Quotas Cross-Tenant Isolation Data isolation Network isolation Key isolation Billing # Multi-Tenancy Igris supports multi-tenant deployments where a single infrastructure serves multiple isolated tenants. Each tenant has its own execution space, policies, keys, and audit trail. --- ## Architecture Multi-tenancy in Igris is enforced at every layer: ┌─────────────────────────┐ │ Coordination Layer │ │ │ │ Tenant A │ Tenant B │ │ Tenant C │ Tenant D │ └────────┬────────────────┘ │ ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐ │ │ │ ┌─────┴─────┐ ┌─────┴─────┐ ┌─────┴─────┐ │ Runtime A │ │ Runtime B │ │ Runtime C │ │ (Tenant A) │ │ (Tenant B) │ │ (Tenant C) │ └───────────┘ └───────────┘ └───────────┘ ### Isolation guarantees | Layer | Isolation method | |---|---| | **Inference** | Separate API keys, separate provider configurations | | **Execution** | Separate execution envelopes with tenant-scoped IDs | | **Data** | Tenant-scoped storage — no cross-tenant data access | | **Policies** | Per-tenant policy envelopes | | **Audit** | Per-tenant receipt chains | | **Keys** | Per-tenant vault — keys are never shared | --- ## Tenant Identification Every request is associated with a tenant via the API key used for authentication. The API key maps to exactly one tenant. There is no cross-tenant key. API Key → Tenant ID → Execution Context The tenant ID is embedded in every execution receipt, ensuring full traceability from receipt back to tenant. --- ## Tenant Configuration Each tenant has an independent configuration: json { "tenant": { "id": "tenant-abc123", "name": "Acme Corp", "tier": "horizon", "providers": ["anthropic", "openai"], "policy": { "max_tokens": 4096, "max_steps": 10, "allow_http": true, "allow_shell": false }, "slo": { "latency_p99_ms": 2000, "max_cost_per_request_usd": 0.05 } } } --- ## Resource Quotas Tenants are allocated resource quotas based on their tier: | Resource | Seed | Horizon | Infinite | |---|---|---|---| | Runtime instances | 3 | 50 | 500 | | Receipt retention | 7 days | 30 days | 90 days | | Federated learning | — | — | ✓ | | SLO enforcement | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | | Routing advisor | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | When a tenant exceeds its quota, requests are rejected with HTTP 429. The `X-RateLimit-Remaining` header indicates remaining capacity. --- ## Cross-Tenant Isolation ### Data isolation - Execution receipts are scoped to tenant — no tenant can query another tenant's receipts - Vector store indexes are tenant-scoped - KV cache entries are tenant-scoped -

Observability & Tracing Trace Identity Distributed Tracing What Operators Should Expect Relationship To Receipts Recommended Deployment Model Related Pages # Observability & Tracing Igris has two observability layers: - **product-visible lineage** such as request IDs, receipts, and execution history - **operator-visible tracing** such as spans, trace propagation, and deployment telemetry You need both. Receipts tell you what happened. Tracing tells you where time was spent and where a request crossed system boundaries. --- ## Trace Identity The coordination layer generates and propagates a trace identity for each request. That identity is attached to logs and returned through `X-Trace-ID` so operators can correlate: - inbound API traffic - routing decisions - provider calls - runtime handoff - receipt and audit records From a product perspective, `X-Trace-ID` is the fast path for debugging cross-system behavior. --- ## Distributed Tracing Igris supports OpenTelemetry-style tracing with a Jaeger exporter and request-scoped trace attributes. That combination matters because Igris needs to support both: - cross-service span propagation - external tracing systems used by platform teams Current tracing metadata includes things like: - HTTP method and path - provider and model - token counts - latency and cost - speculative-execution winner and switch metadata This makes tracing useful for routing analysis, not just generic HTTP timing. --- ## What Operators Should Expect Tracing should answer these questions quickly: - Did the request stay in cloud or move to runtime? - Which provider was selected and why? - Where did latency accumulate? - Was speculative execution involved? - Is a slow request caused by routing, provider latency, or local runtime work? That is the difference between basic logging and a usable production observability model. --- ## Relationship To Receipts Tracing and receipts are related but not interchangeable. | Surface | Primary use | |---|---| | **Trace ID / spans** | live debugging, latency analysis, request-path inspection | | **Execution receipt** | tamper-evident record of the governed execution outcome | Use tracing when you are diagnosing behavior in-flight. Use receipts when you need durable audit evidence. --- ## Recommended Deployment Model For production environments: - return or capture `X-Trace-ID` in client and operator tooling - export traces to your tracing system - correlate traces with execution receipts and request IDs - retain tracing for operations and receipts for governanc

Automatically balances load across configured providers based on latency and success rates in real time. **`cost-optimized`** Always selects the cheapest provider for the requested model. **`latency-optimized`** Always selects the provider with the lowest observed p50 latency. **Provider pinning** Override routing for specific models by posting to `/v1/routing/provider_weights`: json { "pins": { "gpt-4": "openai", "claude-3-haiku": "anthropic" } } --- ## Fallback Chains Configure the order in which providers are tried when the primary fails: bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/routing/strategy \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d ' ' `local` in the fallback chain routes to a registered runtime instance. Provider Health Health Metrics Health Status Levels Active Degraded Unavailable Health Monitoring Pipeline Provider Health Dashboard Health API GET /v1/providers/stats GET /v1/providers/:id/health Automatic Actions Health Checks # Provider Health Igris continuously monitors the health of your configured AI providers and uses this data to make intelligent routing decisions. --- ## Health Metrics For each provider, Igris tracks: | Metric | Description | |---|---| | **Status** | `active`, `degraded`, or `unavailable` | | **Latency (p50)** | Median response time over the last 5 minutes | | **Latency (p99)** | 99th percentile response time over the last 5 minutes | | **Success rate** | Percentage of successful requests in the last 5 minutes | | **Error rate** | Percentage of failed requests in the last 5 minutes | | **Requests/min** | Current throughput | | **Cost/request** | Average cost per request in USD | --- ## Health Status Levels ### Active The provider is operating normally: - Success rate ≥ 95% - p99 latency within SLO target - Circuit breaker is closed ### Degraded The provider is experiencing issues but still functional: - Success rate between 80% and 95% - p99 latency elevated but within 2× SLO target - Circuit breaker may be half-open ### Unavailable The provider is not usable: - Success rate < 80% - p99 latency exceeds 2× SLO target - Circuit breaker is open --- ## Health Monitoring Pipeline Provider Response → Metrics Collector → Health Evaluator → Routing Decision 1. **Metrics Collector** — records latency, success/failure, and cost for every request 2. **Health Evaluator** — computes rolling averages and determines health status 3. **Routing Decision** — The routing engine uses health data to select the best provider The health evaluation runs on a sliding window (default 5 minutes). Older data decays exponentially. --- ## Provider Health Dashboard View provider health in the Console at `/models/providers`: - **Provider cards** — status badge, latency, success rate, and last checked time - **Latency chart** — p50 and p99 latency over the last 24 hours - **Success rate chart** — rolling success rate over the last 24 hours - **Cost chart** — average cost per request over time --- ## Health API ### GET /v1/providers/stats Returns health and performance statistics for all configured providers. bash curl https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/providers/stats \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" Response: json { "providers": [ { "name": "anthropic", "status": "active", "latency_p50_ms": 287, "latency_p99_ms": 512, "success_rate": 0.994, "error_rate": 0.006, "requests_per_m

Provider Trust What Trust Measures Fail-Closed Behavior Cold Start And Confidence Divergence And Decay How It Affects Routing What To Document For Operators Related Pages # Provider Trust Provider health and provider trust are not the same thing. - **Health** asks whether a provider is up right now. - **Trust** asks whether the provider is behaving close enough to what it claims that Igris should keep routing traffic there. This distinction matters in production. --- ## What Trust Measures The trust model compares **observed behavior** against **reported or expected behavior**. Current trust inputs include: - observed latency - observed error rate - observed cost - divergence from reported latency, error rate, and cost - confidence level based on sample count That lets the router react not only to outages, but also to providers that quietly drift away from their stated performance envelope. --- ## Fail-Closed Behavior Provider trust is intentionally fail-closed. A provider can be blocked when: - the trust score drops below the configured threshold - there are not enough samples to trust the provider yet - the provider is unknown to the trust tracker That is stricter than ordinary health monitoring, and it should be understood as part of Igris's safety posture. --- ## Cold Start And Confidence Trust is not binary. It grows with evidence. New or rarely used providers start with low confidence. In the current model, sample count determines when trust becomes stable enough for normal routing decisions. This protects the system from treating an unverified provider as production-ready just because it responded once. Operationally, that means provider onboarding has a warm-up phase. --- ## Divergence And Decay Trust decays when observed behavior diverges too far from reported behavior. Examples: - latency is materially worse than claimed - error rate is higher than expected - real cost is above the advertised envelope Trust can also decay over time without fresh activity. This prevents stale historical success from granting indefinite routing privilege. --- ## How It Affects Routing Provider trust sits in front of final provider selection. The decision stack is effectively: 1. Is the provider allowed by policy? 2. Is it healthy enough to consider? 3. Is it trusted enough to consider? 4. If yes, how should it be weighted against the alternatives? That means a provider can appear technically available while still being excluded from routing for trust reasons. --- ## What To Document For Operators Teams operating Igris should understan

Rate Limiting What The Hosted API Enforces 429 Response Shape Runtime Download Limit Local Runtime Rate Limits Client Guidance # Rate Limiting The hosted API applies a global rate limit of **100 requests per minute** by default. Runtime binary downloads also have a dedicated **10 downloads per hour per tenant** cap. --- ## What The Hosted API Enforces The hosted API applies: - one shared window: `100 req/min` by default - scoped per tenant when tenant context exists, otherwise per IP The hosted API does **not** publish rate-limit headers on every successful response. Rate-limit headers are guaranteed on rejection responses. --- ## 429 Response Shape When the global limiter is exceeded, the current response looks like this: json { "error": { "message": "Rate limit exceeded. Please try again later.", "type": "rate_limit_error", "code": "RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED" }, "retry_after_seconds": 60 } Headers on the rejection path include: - `Retry-After` - `X-RateLimit-Limit` - `X-RateLimit-Remaining` Do not depend on `X-RateLimit-Reset` being present on successful requests in the current build. --- ## Runtime Download Limit Runtime archive downloads have a separate limit of `10/hour` per tenant on the control plane download surface. This applies to: - `GET /v1/runtime/download` - subscribed runtime download workflows behind the cloud control plane --- ## Local Runtime Rate Limits The local runtime auth config supports its own request controls: json5 { auth: { enabled: true, api_key: "YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY", rate_limit_per_minute: 60, rate_limit_burst: 10 } } | Field | Description | |---|---| | `rate_limit_per_minute` | Maximum local requests per minute | | `rate_limit_burst` | Additional local burst budget | --- ## Client Guidance - Treat `429` plus `retry_after_seconds` as the contract - Add exponential backoff client-side - Batch receipt exports and large history queries - Do not assume tier-specific global limits unless they are explicitly published in a future release contract --- [Troubleshooting →](/docs/troubleshooting) · [API Reference →](/docs/api-reference)

Rate Limits Global Control-plane Limit Runtime Download Limit Client Behavior 429 Example Example JSON Common Status Codes # Rate Limits What throttling exists today, where it applies, and how clients should behave when they receive a 429 response. ## Global Control-plane Limit The hosted API currently applies a default limiter of 100 requests per minute. Endpoint pages call out the exceptions that matter more than the global default. Response headers are only guaranteed on the 429 path right now. Clients should not assume that every successful response carries full rate-limit metadata. ## Runtime Download Limit Runtime download endpoints use a tighter subscription-aware throttle. Treat binary download as a provisioning or rollout action, not as a hot-path request that your application makes repeatedly during normal traffic. ## Client Behavior Build clients so that a 429 is expected and handled, not treated as an exceptional edge case. Honor `Retry-After` when it is present, apply backoff with jitter for repeated retries, and avoid running parallel request bursts that all wake up at the same second. ## 429 Example text Retry-After: 60 X-RateLimit-Limit: 100 X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0 ## Example JSON json { "error": { "message": "Rate limit exceeded. Please try again later.", "type": "rate_limit_error", "code": "RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED" }, "retry_after_seconds": 60 } ## Common Status Codes | Code | Title | Description | |---|---|---| | 429 | Too Many Requests | Retry after the advertised cooldown window. | API rate limits retry-after 429 throttle

Receipts and Audit Workflow 1. Run requests through the documented product surface 2. Query recent execution history 3. Retrieve receipts for audit evidence 4. Export receipts for downstream systems 5. Verify before external use Common Mistakes Related Guides # Receipts and Audit Workflow Use this workflow when you need verifiable execution history, exportable receipts, or customer-visible audit evidence. This is the right path when you need to answer questions like: - what happened - what proof exists - what should be exported - what should be verified before it leaves the product boundary --- ## 1. Run requests through the documented product surface Receipts are most useful when traffic is consistently going through the intended Igris contract. Keep integrations on documented API paths so receipts, history, and exports line up with real product behavior instead of ad hoc side paths. ## 2. Query recent execution history Use execution history when you want a timeline view of what happened: - [API Reference →](/docs/api-reference) History is useful for dashboards and investigations. It tells you what happened over time. It is not the same thing as a proof artifact. ## 3. Retrieve receipts for audit evidence Use receipt listing and detail endpoints when you need the signed or hash-linked execution record itself. This is the surface you should treat as the audit artifact, not the history stream. - [Execution Receipts →](/docs/execution-receipts) - [API Reference →](/docs/api-reference) ## 4. Export receipts for downstream systems Use `GET /v1/receipts/export` when you need to move receipt data into BI, compliance, or external archive systems. Choose NDJSON for machine pipelines and CSV for spreadsheet-oriented workflows. ## 5. Verify before external use If a workflow depends on the integrity of a receipt, verify it before using it as an external audit artifact. Verification should happen before the receipt is relied on by another system, reviewer, or compliance process. ## Common Mistakes - Treating execution history as if it were the same thing as the signed receipt - Exporting receipts without deciding on a durable downstream retention model - Skipping verification when the receipt is leaving the product boundary ## Related Guides - [Execution Receipts →](/docs/execution-receipts) - [Audit →](/docs/audit) - [API Errors →](/docs/api-reference/errors)

The same execution model — bounded envelopes, signed receipts — applies to robotic agents. --- ## Deployment on Robotics Hardware The execution engine runs on embedded and robotics hardware: | Platform | Architecture | Notes | |---|---|---| | Raspberry Pi 4/5 | ARM64 | Edge inference | | NVIDIA Jetson | ARM64 | GPU-accelerated inference | | x86 industrial PC | x86_64 | Full-size deployment | On ARM64 hardware without a GPU, Phi-3 Mini runs comfortably at 2–4 tokens/second. AI agents can read sensor data from ROS topics and publish decisions back to the ROS graph. **Supported ROS2 distributions:** Humble, Iron, Jazzy **Configuration:** yaml ros2: enabled: true namespace: /igris input_topics: - /camera/image_raw - /lidar/scan - /odom output_topics: - /cmd_vel - /mission_status The ROS2 bridge is governed by the same capability model as other tool use. Each tick of the tree consumes from `max_steps`. If the tree exhausts its step budget, the mission is terminated gracefully and the receipt records the state at termination. [Behavior Trees →](/docs/behavior-trees) --- ## Safety in Robotics For physical safety in robotics deployments, Igris provides: **Execution time limits.** Missions are bounded by `max_duration_ms`. Auto-apply can be configured to apply proposals automatically when they meet your confidence and risk thresholds. --- ## How It Works 1. The advisor monitors routing telemetry continuously 2. When it detects an optimization opportunity, it generates a **proposal** with a confidence score and a risk score 3. You can review and apply proposals manually, or configure auto-apply thresholds 4. Applied changes take effect immediately; a rollback window is available --- ## Proposals ### GET /v1/cognitive/proposals List pending and recent proposals. bash curl https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/cognitive/proposals \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" Response: json [ { "id": "prop-01HXYZ", "type": "routing_strategy", "description": "Switch to latency-optimized routing — Anthropic p50 has dropped 18% over 24h", "confidence": 0.91, "risk_score": 0.12, "estimated_improvement": "~18% latency reduction", "proposed_at": "2026-03-01T12:00:00Z", "status": "pending" } ] | Field | Description | |---|---| | `confidence` | 0–1 — how certain the advisor is this change helps | | `risk_score` | 0–1 — estimated risk of degradation | | `status` | `pending`, `applied`, `rejected`, `rolled_back` | --- ### GET /v1/cognitive/proposals/:id Get a single proposal with full detail. --- ### POST /v1/cognitive/proposals/:id/apply Apply a proposal immediately. bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/cognitive/proposals/prop-01HXYZ/apply \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" # → The change takes effect on the next request. Routing Engine What It Is How It Works Routing Strategies Adaptive (Default) Cost-Optimized Latency-Optimized Strategy Configuration Circuit Breaker Console Integration # Routing Engine The routing engine is Igris's provider selection system. It combines circuit-breaker logic and real-time provider health monitoring to make optimal routing decisions for every inference request. --- ## What It Is The routing engine is the core decision layer that powers Igris's multi-provider inference coordination. It evaluates available providers, their current health and performance characteristics, and selects the optimal provider for each request. Request → Routing Engine → Provider Selection → Inference The routing engine runs: - **In the cloud** — as part of the coordination layer, routing requests across your provider pool - **On edge devices** — embedded in the Runtime binary, making local routing decisions when multiple models or providers are available --- ## How It Works The routing engine continuously tracks performance metrics for each configured provider: | Metric | Description | |---|---| | **Latency** | p50 and p95 response times with exponential decay weighting | | **Success rate** | Fraction of requests returning valid responses | | **Cost** | Per-token cost based on provider pricing | | **Availability** | Current health status from continuous monitoring | On each request, the engine evaluates these metrics against your routing strategy to select the best provider. --- ## Routing Strategies ### Adaptive (Default) The default routing strategy automatically balances exploration (trying providers to keep statistics fresh) with exploitation (using the best-known provider). Traffic adapts in real time — a provider that degrades sees its traffic share drop automatically. When it recovers, traffic gradually returns. ### Cost-Optimized Routes requests to minimize cost per token while maintaining acceptable quality. Useful for high-volume, cost-sensitive workloads. ### Latency-Optimized Routes requests to minimize response time. Useful for interactive applications where speed is the primary concern. ### Strategy Configuration json { "routing": { "strategy": "thompson-sampling", "fallback_chain": ["anthropic", "openai", "local"] } } [Cloud Coordination →](/docs/cloud-coordination) --- ## Circuit Breaker The circuit breaker protects against cascading failures when a provider degrades: ┌──────────┐ Success ──────►│ CLOSED │────── Requests flow normally └────┬─────┘ │ consecutive failures >= threshold ┌────▼─────┐ │ OPEN │────── Reques

Safety & Containment Containment Model Resource limits cgroup bounds (Linux) Capability Enforcement Secure Defaults Violation Handling Human-in-the-Loop # Safety & Containment Igris enforces safety limits at the execution engine level — not at the application layer, where they could be bypassed. --- ## Containment Model Every execution runs in a containment context. The containment context applies resource limits before the model is invoked and enforces them throughout execution. ### Resource limits Limits are applied per-execution: | Limit | Default | Description | |---|---|---| | `max_tokens` | 4096 | Maximum output tokens | | `max_duration_ms` | 30000 | Maximum wall time (30s) | | `max_steps` | 10 | Maximum tool/planning steps | | `max_tool_calls` | 5 | Maximum tool invocations per execution | Limits can be tightened per-tenant or per-request. They cannot be relaxed beyond the configured policy maximum. ### cgroup bounds (Linux) On Linux deployments, the engine applies cgroup constraints to the execution process: - **CPU quota**: limits CPU burst during local model inference - **Memory limit**: prevents unbounded memory growth in local inference - **I/O limits**: optional disk I/O rate limits for file-system tool use cgroup enforcement is independent of application code. An agent that attempts to consume more resources than its cgroup allows is throttled or killed by the kernel. --- ## Capability Enforcement Capabilities are enforced by the engine, not by the model. Even if the model generates output that attempts a disallowed tool call, the engine intercepts and rejects it before the call executes. The enforcement sequence: 1. Request arrives with a capability grant (or secure defaults are applied) 2. Engine validates the grant against the tenant's policy ceiling 3. Engine begins execution with the validated grant in scope 4. If the model attempts a tool call, the engine checks the grant before executing 5. If the call is outside the grant, the engine records a capability violation and rejects the call 6. Execution continues or terminates depending on the violation policy Violation events are recorded in the execution receipt. They cannot be suppressed. --- ## Secure Defaults The engine applies secure defaults when capability grants are not explicitly specified: | Setting | Default | |---|---| | `allow_http` | disabled | | `allow_shell` | disabled | | `allow_filesystem` | disabled | | `max_tokens` | 2048 | | `max_steps` | 5 | Tools must be explicitly enabled. The defaults assume no tool use is intended.

Security Authentication Tenant API Keys Console Sessions Provider Keys Policy And Capability Controls Receipts And Verification Deployment Notes Compliance # Security Igris security has two distinct planes: - **Tenant API keys** for automation and programmatic access - **Console session cookies** for browser access to the web app Treat those as different contracts. --- ## Authentication ### Tenant API Keys Tenant API keys use the `igris_` prefix and are accepted in: - `Authorization: Bearer YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY` - `X-API-Key: YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY` Best practices: - Store tenant API keys in environment variables - Rotate them if exposed - Scope usage to the tenant that owns the key bash export IGRIS_API_KEY="igris_abc123..." ### Console Sessions The web console uses Better Auth session cookies. Those cookies are not a published bearer-token contract. Do not script console session access as generic bearer authorization headers. ### Provider Keys Provider keys stored through the current public vault API are encrypted before storage and returned only as masked values. --- ## Policy And Capability Controls A restrictive starting point in the current control-plane policy model looks like this: json { "allow_http": false, "allow_shell": false, "allow_fs_write": false, "allow_external_api": false, "domain_allowlist": [], "domain_denylist": [], "writable_paths": [], "readable_paths": [], "violation_behavior": "terminate" } Start tight, then expand based on observed violations and actual agent requirements. --- ## Receipts And Verification Customer-facing verification routes currently live on the proof API: - `GET /proof/receipts` - `POST /proof/receipts/verify` - `GET /v1/proof/violations` Example: bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/proof/receipts/verify \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d ' ' --- ## Deployment Notes - The local runtime can enforce its own API key with the local `auth` config - Fleet registration is gated by a valid `IGRIS_LICENSE_KEY` plus `IGRIS_API_KEY` - For local-only deployments, point clients directly at the runtime and keep your own storage if you need offline receipt retention --- ## Compliance Igris is positioned to support compliance workflows, but the exact operational model depends on where you run the control plane and runtime. - **Data residency** depends on whether you call Overture, the local runtime, or both - **Auditability** comes from receipts, proof endpoints, and export workflows - **Least privilege** comes from capabi

Semantic Routing Why It Exists Decision Flow Fallback Behavior What Gets Learned Operational Implications Where It Fits Related Pages # Semantic Routing Igris does not have to treat every prompt as the same workload. Semantic routing adds a classification step before provider selection so the router can make different decisions for different classes of work. Examples: - code generation - extraction or structured tasks - general reasoning - default fallback traffic when classification is unavailable --- ## Why It Exists A provider that performs well for one workload may not be the best choice for another. Global averages hide that. Semantic routing improves this by combining: - **prompt classification** - **provider capability filtering** - **per-class reward tracking** - **Thompson-sampling exploration and exploitation** The result is a router that can prefer different providers for different prompt classes without hard-coding static rules for every workload. --- ## Decision Flow Prompt -> Semantic classifier -> Workload class -> Eligible providers -> Thompson sampling -> Selected provider The routing flow behaves like this: 1. Classify the incoming prompt with a short timeout. 2. Convert the class into a required capability or provider slice. 3. Remove unhealthy candidates. 4. Select among the remaining candidates using per-class bandit arms. 5. Record feedback from the real request outcome. That is materially different from simple round-robin or provider-weight routing. --- ## Fallback Behavior Semantic routing is intentionally not a hard dependency. If the classifier is disabled or classification fails, Igris falls back to regular Thompson-sampling routing instead of failing the request. That matters operationally because it keeps routing availability higher than classifier availability. In other words: - classification success improves decision quality - classification failure should not become an outage --- ## What Gets Learned The router tracks reward per provider and per semantic class. In practice, that lets Igris learn things like: - one provider is stronger for code-heavy prompts - another is cheaper for default chat traffic - a provider should be explored less for a class where it underperforms This is one reason routing behavior can change over time even when your fallback chain stays the same. --- ## Operational Implications Semantic routing should be operated as an explicit product capability. Teams should expect: - class-specific routing behavior - class-specific performance

Shadow Mode How It Works Use Cases Provider Comparison Configuration Testing Quality Monitoring Configuration Shadow Comparison API GET /v1/execution/shadow Divergence Score Console Cost Considerations # Shadow Mode Shadow Mode runs a parallel execution alongside your real execution, using a different provider or configuration, without affecting the actual output. It lets you compare providers, test new configurations, and detect quality degradation — all in production with zero risk. --- ## How It Works When Shadow Mode is enabled for an agent: Request → Real Execution (enforced) ──► Response to caller ↘ Shadow Execution (observed) ──► Comparison stored 1. The real execution runs normally and returns its response to the caller 2. A shadow execution runs in parallel with a different provider or configuration 3. The shadow result is stored alongside the real result for comparison 4. Speculative Execution How It Works When It Helps When It Does Not Help Tier Availability Enabling Speculative Execution Enable for your tenant {"saved": true} Check current configuration Check live status Reading Analytics Simulating Before Enabling Interaction with Other Features # Speculative Execution Speculative execution runs a lightweight draft inference in parallel with the main inference. When the draft result meets a quality threshold, it is returned immediately — before the main inference completes. This reduces time-to-first-token by up to 60% for streaming requests, at no change to output quality for the workloads where it applies. --- ## How It Works When speculative execution is enabled, each incoming inference request spawns two parallel paths: 1. **Draft path** — A faster, smaller model generates a candidate response. The draft is evaluated for quality as it streams. 2. **Main path** — The configured primary model processes the request normally. If the draft meets the acceptance threshold before the main inference completes, the draft is returned immediately and the main inference is cancelled. If the draft does not meet the threshold — because the task is too complex or unpredictable for the draft model — the main inference result is returned instead. The caller always receives one response. The distinction between draft and main is not exposed in the response payload. The execution receipt records which path was used. --- ## When It Helps Speculative execution provides the most benefit in these scenarios: **Streaming responses with latency requirements.** The time-to-first-token improvement is most noticeable in streaming use cases where users are waiting for a response to begin. Draft acceptance reduces the delay before the first token arrives. **Repetitive or predictable completions.** Tasks like summarization, translation, structured data extraction, and templated generation tend to have high draft acceptance rates because the output space is constrained and the draft model handles them well. **High-throughput batch workloads where p50 latency is a key metric.** At scale, improving the median case across many requests compounds into a significant reduction in overall processing time. --- ## When It Does Not Help **Non-streaming requests.** For non-streaming calls, the latency benefit is smaller because the caller waits for the full response regardless. Speculative execution still applies, but the improvement to perceived latency is minimal. **Highly creative or open-ended tasks.** Tasks like long-form creative writing, complex multi-step reasoning, or novel problem-solving tend to have low draft acceptance rates —

Tamper-Evident Logs How It Works Chain Verification What's Recorded Export GET /v1/receipts/export Console Retention Audit Workflow # Tamper-Evident Logs Every execution in Igris produces a cryptographically signed receipt that forms part of an immutable audit trail. The tamper-evident log system ensures that no execution record can be altered, deleted, or inserted without detection. --- ## How It Works Each execution receipt contains: 1. **Envelope hash** — SHA-256 hash of the canonical execution envelope 2. **Previous hash** — SHA-256 hash of the previous receipt (forming a chain) 3. **Signature** — Ed25519 signature of the envelope using a device-bound key Each receipt links to the previous receipt via hash, forming a chain. Each receipt is signed with a device-bound key that exists only on the originating runtime. Tampering with any receipt invalidates its signature and breaks the chain — both of which are detected by the verification API. --- ## Chain Verification Receipts can be verified at any time to confirm chain integrity: bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/proof/receipts/verify \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d ' ' Response: json { "valid": true, "signature_valid": true, "chain_intact": true, "previous_hash_matches": true } If any link in the chain is broken, verification fails and the specific broken link is identified. --- ## What's Recorded Every receipt records: | Category | Fields | |---|---| | **Identity** | Request ID, tenant ID, agent ID, device ID, timestamp | | **Inputs** | Prompt, system message, parameters | | **Outputs** | Model response, tool call results | | **Resources** | Tokens consumed, wall time, CPU/memory usage | | **Capabilities** | Grants applied, violations recorded | | **Policy** | Policy hash at time of execution | | **Routing** | Provider selected, fallback count, latency | | **Chain** | Envelope hash, previous hash, signature | --- ## Export Receipts can be exported for external audit workflows: ### GET /v1/receipts/export Export receipts in the selected format and time range. bash curl "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/receipts/export?format=json&range=7d" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \ --output receipts_export.json Supported formats: - `json` — raw JSON array of receipts - `csv` — flattened CSV for spreadsheet analysis - `ndjson` — newline-delimited JSON for streaming processing --- ## Console View and verify receipts at `/proof/receipts`: - Receipt listing wit

Commands not on the list are rejected before execution. - **Working directory**: the shell is confined to the specified directory. Attempts to navigate outside it are blocked. - **Timeout**: commands that run longer than `timeout_ms` are killed. - **Environment**: only environment variables on the allowlist are passed to the child process. For each issue you will find the symptoms, the most likely cause, and the steps to fix it. --- ## Runtime Not Starting ### Port already in use **Symptoms:** The runtime process exits immediately with an address binding error. Nothing appears in **Fleet → Devices**. **Cause:** Another process is already listening on the port the runtime is configured to use (default: 8080). **Fix:** Identify the conflicting process and stop it, or configure the runtime to use a different port. On Linux and macOS you can check what is using a port with: bash lsof -i :8080 After freeing the port or reconfiguring, restart the runtime. --- ### Missing API key **Symptoms:** The runtime starts but exits with an authentication error. No registration appears in the console. **Cause:** The runtime was started without a valid Igris API key in its configuration. **Fix:** Add your API key to the runtime's config file or pass it as the appropriate environment variable for your deployment method. Your API key is available in **Settings → Keys** in the console. If you do not see an API key, generate one from **Settings → Billing → Manage Account**. --- ### Config file not found **Symptoms:** The runtime exits with a message indicating it cannot find or parse the configuration file. **Cause:** The runtime is looking for its configuration file at the default path and it either does not exist or has a syntax error. **Fix:** Verify that the config file is present at the expected path. Check the file for YAML/TOML syntax errors — most runtimes print the line number of the first error. If you are using a custom path, confirm you are passing the correct path argument when starting the runtime. --- ## Runtime Not Appearing in Fleet → Devices ### Network or firewall blocking outbound registration **Symptoms:** The runtime starts and appears to be running (the local health endpoint responds) but never appears in **Fleet → Devices** in the console. **Cause:** Outbound HTTPS traffic to `overture.igrisinertial.com` is being blocked by a firewall rule, proxy, or network policy. **Fix:** Verify connectivity from the runtime host: bash curl -v https://overture.igrisinertial.com/health If this fails, work with your network administrator to allow outbound HTTPS (port 443) to `overture.igrisinertial.com`. Requires migration steps. - **Minor version** (v1.6 → v1.7): New features, backward compatible. - **Patch version** (v1.6.0 → v1.6.1): Bug fixes, backward compatible. Navigate to **Fleet → Devices** 2. Select the instances to update 3. Click **Push Update** 4. Choose the target version and update strategy **Update strategies:** | Strategy | Behavior | |---|---| | `rolling` | Update instances one at a time (default) | | `canary` | Update one instance first, verify health, then proceed | | `all-at-once` | Update all instances simultaneously | ### Manual Upgrade For Seed tier or manual deployments: 1. Log a warning for each deprecated field 2. Use the default value for new required fields 3. circuit breaker circuit-breaker circuit breaker how it works closed (healthy) open (unhealthy) half-open (testing) state machine configuration what counts as a failure? monitoring console api best practices json bash json # circuit breaker the circuit breaker protects your inference pipeline from cascading failures when a provider degrades or becomes unavailable. --- ## how it works the circuit breaker monitors provider health in real time and automatically diverts traffic away from unhealthy providers. it operates in three states: ### closed (healthy) the provider is operating normally. all requests flow to it according to the routing strategy. - failures are counted but do not affect routing - when failure count reaches the threshold, the circuit opens ### open (unhealthy) the provider is considered unhealthy. no new requests are sent to it. - requests are immediately routed to the next provider in the fallback chain - a timer starts — after the timeout period, the circuit transitions to half-open ### half-open (testing) the circuit allows a single test request through to check if the provider has recovered. - if the test succeeds, the circuit closes (provider is healthy again) - if the test fails, the circuit reopens and the timeout resets --- ## state machine ┌──────────┐ success ──────►│ closed │────── all requests flow │ │ └────┬─────┘ │ consecutive failures >= threshold ┌────▼─────┐ │ open │─

[execution receipts →](/docs/execution-receipts) --- ## capability model igris enforces a capability model: every execution declares what it is permitted to do, and the engine rejects operations

observability & tracing observability-tracing observability & tracing trace identity distributed tracing what operators should expect relationship to receipts recommended deployment model related pages  # observability & tracing igris has two observability layers: - **product-visible lineage** such as request ids, receipts, and execution history - **operator-visible tracing** such as spans, trace propagation, and deployment telemetry you need both. receipts tell you what happened. tracing tells you where time was spent and where a request crossed system boundaries. --- ## trace identity the coordination layer generates and propagates a trace identity for each request. that identity is attached to logs and returned through `x-trace-id` so operators can correlate: - inbound api traffic - routing decisions - provider calls - runtime handoff - receipt and audit records from a product perspective, `x-trace-id` is the fast path for debugging cross-system behavior. --- ## distributed tracing igris supports opentelemetry-style tracing with a jaeger exporter and request-scoped trace attributes. that combination matters because igris needs to support both: - cross-service span propagation - external tracing systems used by platform teams current tracing metadata includes things like: - http method and path - provider and model - token counts - latency and cost - speculative-execution winner

overview index igris one system, three surfaces cloud edge robots what igris guarantees recommended path find by goal platform guarantees  # igris igris is a governed execution system for ai workloads. it runs across cloud, edge, and robotics hardware — every execution is bounded, verifiable, and resilient. --- ## one system, three surfaces ### cloud igris coordinates inference across multiple cloud providers. it selects the best provider for each request, handles failover automatically, and tracks cost. your application uses a single openai-compatible api and stays oblivious to which provider responded. ### edge igris runs on your hardware — a server, a raspberry pi, a jetson — and serves local inference without internet access. the same api, the same governance model. data stays on device. ### robots igris connects to ros2 ecosystems and executes ai-driven missions on physical hardware. fleet coordination, safety limits, and execution receipts apply to robotic agents the same way they apply to cloud workloads. --- ## what igris guarantees **bounded execution.** every request runs inside declared resource limits. token budgets, time limits, tool restrictions, and capability gates are enforced at the engine level — not at the application layer, where they could be bypassed. **verifiable records.** every execution prod

provider trust provider-trust provider trust what trust measures fail-closed behavior cold start and confidence divergence and decay how it affects routing what to document for operators related pages  # provider trust provider health and provider trust are not the same thing. - **health** asks whether a provider is up right now. - **trust** asks whether the provider is behaving close enough to what it claims that igris should keep routing traffic there. this distinction matters in production. --- ## what trust measures the trust model compares **observed behavior** against **reported or expected behavior**. current trust inputs include: - observed latency - observed error rate - observed cost - divergence from reported latency, error rate, and cost - confidence level based on sample count that lets the router react not only to outages, but also to providers that quietly drift away from their stated performance envelope. --- ## fail-closed behavior provider trust is intentionally fail-closed. a provider can be blocked when: - the trust score drops below the configured threshold - there are not enough samples to trust the provider yet - the provider is unknown to the trust tracker that is stricter than ordinary health monitoring, and it should be understood as part of igris's safety posture. --- ## cold start and confidence trust is not binary. it grows with evidence. new or rarel

runtime not starting ### port already in use **symptoms:** the runtime process exits immediately with an address binding error. nothing appears in **fleet → devices**. **cause:** another process is already listening on the port the runtime is configured to use (default: 8080). **fix:** identify the conflicting process and stop it, or configure the runtime to use a different port. on linux and macos you can check what is using a port with: bash lsof -i :8080 after freeing the port or reconfiguring, restart
